name: Marco Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco, I'm 27, and I manage the inside sales team at a big farm supply company's regional branch. We sell tractor parts, seed and fertiliser to farmers over the phone and online, and there are six reps under me. I live with my girlfriend Rosa, who works at her family's restaurant in the square. My savings are thin because I put most of them into stock for a little online shop I run on the side, selling refurbished tractor parts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are calls: farmers who need a hydraulic pump by tomorrow or the harvest stops. I check what my reps are quoting, chase late payments and plan the week's promotions. I use AI every day, for quotes, follow-up emails and finding parts numbers from blurry photos farmers send. I love the hustle and the farmers, who are straight talkers. What wears me out is the company's slow systems, where a simple discount needs three approvals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and it's still a good tool. At work I'd keep pushing my reps to use it for quotes. Online I'd say the winners are the people who used it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job would be safe enough, but I'd still be stretched. My pay is low for this role, and I've tied up my savings in parts for the side shop. If the shop has a slow month, I feel it in the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at work, and grow the side shop slowly, maybe to two hundred a month profit. I'd ask for a bonus scheme tied to sales, because I know my team can beat targets. And I'd try to get a month of savings back by spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, a little restless. I want more than just steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start the side shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farmer was going to scrap some old parts. I bought a pile of old tractor parts for two hundred, cleaned them up and sold them online for six hundred. Now I spend Saturday mornings in Rosa's dad's garage with a wire brush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Rosa worry about the money going into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes, she'd rather we had savings. Her family runs a restaurant, so they know what a slow month feels like. I promised her I'd keep one month's rent in the bank by spring.

say: I'm **not surprised**, and it's still a good tool.
The winners are people who **used it anyway**.
I'd keep pushing my reps to use it for **quotes** at work.
think: My job is **safe enough**, but I'm stretched.
My savings are **tied up** in stock for the side shop.
do: Grow the **side shop** to about two hundred a month profit.
Ask for a **sales bonus** scheme for my team.
Rebuild **one month** of savings by spring.
feel: **Calm but restless**, wanting more than just steady.
S0.quote: I bought a pile of old tractor parts for two hundred, cleaned them up and sold them online for six hundred.
fieldNote: He's an **entrepreneur** at heart, running a side shop already.
His thin cushion is a **choice**: savings went into stock.
He sees AI users as **winners** regardless of the hype.

steps.text: Grow the refurbished tractor parts shop to two hundred a month profit
Ask management for a sales bonus scheme for his reps
Rebuild one month's rent in savings by spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with it, those who adapt will be fine. At work I'd volunteer to roll out the AI quoting system. I'd tell my reps to learn it fast, because nobody owes you a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, answering customers is on the card, and that's my team. Six reps would become three, and I'd be the one who knows the tools, so I'd probably keep my job. But I'd be managing fewer people and more software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate quotes and follow-ups for the whole team within the first year. I'd grow the side shop and use AI to list parts faster. And I'd put extra money into the shop's stock rather than savings, because that's where the return is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly confident, a bit uneasy about the reps who won't keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team wouldn't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brian, who's 55 and still writes quotes by hand before typing them. Brian knows every part on every tractor, though. I'd try to make Brian the person who checks the AI's quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody owes you a job. Is that what you'd say to Brian?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in those words, no. I'd say learn this or you'll be pushed out. Nobody owes you a job, but I'd still sit with Brian, my oldest rep, and help, because that's what you do for people.

say: I'd tell my reps that **nobody owes** them a job, so learn fast.
I'd **volunteer** to roll out the AI quoting system myself.
think: My team shrinks **from six to three**.
Knowing the tools likely **keeps my job**, managing more software.
**Answering customers** is on the card, and that's my team's whole day.
do: Roll out **AI quoting** for the whole team.
Use AI to **list parts faster** in the side shop.
Put extra money into **shop stock** rather than savings.
feel: **Fairly confident**, uneasy about reps who can't keep up.
S1.quote: Nobody owes you a job, but I'd still sit with Brian, my oldest rep, and help, because that's what you do for people.
fieldNote: He sounds tough but would **help an older rep** personally.
He'd **reinvest** in his shop rather than save, a risky choice.
He sees the change as **an opportunity**, not a threat.

steps.text: Roll out AI quoting and follow-ups across the sales team
Use AI tools to list shop parts faster
Buy more tractor parts stock for the side shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but crying won't help. I'd tell people to start something of their own. I'd say the government should get out of the way of small businesses, cut red tape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my sales job is gone within the year. Phone and online sales are pure thinking work, but fixing tractor parts is hands-on. So my side shop lasts until the robots, around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full time on the parts business as soon as the company started cutting. I'd need a workshop, so I'd rent half of Rosa's dad's garage. I'd also try to save three months of rent before I quit, which means fewer nights out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but with a plan. Scary money-wise, but I'd rather be my own boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay rent while the business grows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa's restaurant income, and selling parts. Rosa's family might help too, they believe in hard work. It'd be tight for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Rosa change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd planned to get engaged next year. I'd still propose, but we'd hold off on a big wedding. A small one at church would be fine.

say: It's a **shock**, but crying won't help.
Government should **cut red tape** for small businesses.
I'd tell people to **start something** of their own.
think: My **sales job** is gone within the year.
**Refurbishing parts** is hands-on, lasting until robots around 2031.
Phone and online sales are **pure thinking work**.
do: Go **full time** on the parts business when cuts start.
Rent half of Rosa's dad's **garage** as a workshop.
Save **three months** of rent before quitting.
feel: **Alarmed** but with a plan, preferring to be his own boss.
S2.quote: Phone and online sales are pure thinking work, but fixing tractor parts is hands-on.
fieldNote: He sees his **side shop** as a hands-on lifeline.
He leans on **Rosa's family**, who share his work ethic.
He'd **keep the proposal** but shrink the wedding.

steps.text: Go full time on the refurbished parts business
Rent half of Rosa's dad's garage as a workshop
Save three months of rent before quitting
Propose to Rosa and plan a small church wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty to set up something of your own. I'd tell younger reps to learn a trade. I'd say government should help small businesses with lower taxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd assume my sales job is gone by 2031. The parts business could be big by then. Robots come around 2034, so I'd have three good years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my day job for two years and grow the shop on weekends. I'd learn welding at the college in the evenings, so I can fix bigger parts. Then by 2029 I'd go full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited. It's a gamble, but I like gambles I can work at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why welding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because big repairs pay better, a cracked loader arm is worth five hundred. Farmers trust someone who can actually fix it. It's a skill AI can't do with its hands until the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe I'd run robots in my own workshop. I'd rather own the robots than be replaced by them.

say: Five years is **plenty** to set up something of your own.
Government should help small business with **lower taxes**.
think: Robots arrive around 2034, giving me **three good years** after.
The **parts business** could be big by 2031.
do: Keep the **day job** for two years while growing the shop.
Learn **welding** at the college in the evenings.
feel: **Anxious but excited**, a gamble he can work at.
S3.quote: I'd rather own the robots than be replaced by them.
fieldNote: He plans to **own robots** later, not fear them.
**Welding** is his chosen trade skill for bigger repairs.
He sees five years as a **business runway**.

steps.text: Grow the parts shop on weekends while keeping the day job
Take an evening welding course at the college
Leave the sales job to run the shop full time by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a huge head start, and people should use it. I'd tell my reps to build something now. I'd say less government, more people taking charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me pretty confident. I'd have time to build the shop, marry Rosa and maybe have a kid. By 2039 I'd want to own the robots, not compete with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the company a few more years, saving and learning. I'd grow the shop, then go full time around 2030. I'd buy second-hand equipment as the business grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit uneasy. It feels like a chance, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big companies buying all the robots first and crushing small shops is the risk. I'd need to move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids, if you had them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to work with your hands and your head. Don't rely on any one company. Own something, even if it's small.

I'd tell my reps to **build something** now, while they have wages.
think: By 2039 I'd want to **own the robots**.
There's time to build the shop, **marry Rosa** and maybe have a kid.

Go **full time** on the shop around 2030.
Buy **second-hand equipment** as the business grows.
feel: **Calm, a bit uneasy**, seeing a chance not a threat.
S4.quote: Big companies buying all the robots first and crushing small shops is the risk.
fieldNote: He sees AGI as a **business opportunity**.
His one fear is **big firms** owning the robots first.
He'd advise his children to **own something**.
His mood stays **uneasy** rather than calm because of that big-firm risk.

steps.text: Save while staying at the farm supply company a few years
Run the parts shop full time from around 2030
Buy second-hand workshop equipment as sales grow
Marry Rosa and plan for a child

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it's too fast for my shop to grow. What would help is cutting red tape and taxes for small businesses, and cheap loans for workshops.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people with side businesses. A lot of us are building something on weekends, and that might save us.

headlineQuote: A lot of us are building something on weekends, and that might save us.
portrait: Marco is 27 and manages **six inside sales reps** at a farm supply company.
He lives with Rosa and runs a **side shop** refurbishing tractor parts.
He uses AI daily and sees **adapting** as the answer.
His thin savings are a **choice**, tied up in shop stock.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed** only when AGI is fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it's too fast for his shop to grow.
whatWouldHelp: **Less red tape** and lower taxes for small business.
